<!-- STEP id="weight" -->
## Weight: Earth's Pull, Made Precise

Every object near Earth's surface is pulled downward by gravity. That downward pull is its **weight** — a force, measured in newtons, not just "how heavy something feels."

<!-- STEP id="formula" -->
## Putting a Number on It

Weight follows a simple rule: **weight = mass x g**, where g is about 9.8 N of pull for every kilogram of mass.

A 2 kg object weighs about 2 x 9.8 = **19.6 N**.

<!-- STEP id="water" -->
## An Upward Push From the Water

Put an object in water, and something new appears: the water itself pushes back, upward. This is the **buoyant force**.

A small, dense steel ball barely pushes any water aside — so the buoyant force on it stays small. It sinks.

<!-- STEP id="compare" -->
## Which Wins?

The ball's weight is bigger than the buoyant force pushing back on it. **Weight wins, so it sinks.**

<!-- STEP id="recap" -->
## Same Steel, Reshaped

Spread that exact same amount of steel into a wide, hollow hull, and it pushes aside far more water.

**Now the buoyant force is enough to match the steel's full weight — so it floats, same steel and all.**
